procedural_history.originating_court: Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Madras Bench
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated the 23rd day of February 1951 of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Madras Bench in Reference Applications Nos. 312, 310 and 311 of 1950-51.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Madras High Court issued a judgment and order dated the 10th day of March 1952 in C.M.P. Nos. 10427, 10425 and 10426 of 1951.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The matter came before the Supreme Court by way of special appeal (Civil Appeals Nos. 124 to 126 of 1954) after special leave was granted to appeal the Madras High Court's judgment and order.

issue.issue_text: Whether an inference from established facts is, by its nature, a question of law and therefore open to review by the court.

law.statement: The court established a distinction between a 'pure question of fact' and a 'mixed question of law and fact'.

An inference drawn from established facts is considered a question of law only when the issue being decided is a 'mixed question of law and fact'. This occurs when the ultimate finding requires the application of legal principles to the established facts.

Conversely, if the issue is a 'pure question of fact', the final determination, even if it is an inference from other basic facts, remains a question of fact and does not involve the application of any legal principle.

application.law_applied: The court established a distinction between a 'pure question of fact' and a 'mixed question of law and fact'.
application.application_text: The court analyzed the appellant's argument and the supporting case law, noting that the authorities cited (such as English decisions and Privy Council cases) did not support the broad contention that *all* inferences from facts are questions of law. Instead, those cases dealt with situations where the ultimate conclusion was a 'mixed question of law and fact'—for example, whether a transaction was an 'adventure in the nature of trade', which requires applying a legal definition to the facts.

application.law_applied: An inference drawn from established facts is considered a question of law only when the issue being decided is a 'mixed question of law and fact'. This occurs when the ultimate finding requires the application of legal principles to the established facts.
application.application_text: The court explained that in cases of mixed questions of law and fact, the ultimate finding is an inference drawn from the facts found, but it is reached through 'the application of the proper principles of law'. In such instances, it is correct to say the inference is a question of law.

application.law_applied: Conversely, if the issue is a 'pure question of fact', the final determination, even if it is an inference from other basic facts, remains a question of fact and does not involve the application of any legal principle.
application.application_text: The court used an illustration of a suit on a promissory note where the defense is denial of execution. The court might find subsidiary facts (e.g., the signature is unlike others, witnesses were not present) and from these, infer that the note is not genuine. This entire process, from finding basic facts to drawing the final conclusion, is a determination of a pure question of fact, as no legal principle is applied to reach the conclusion.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's broad contention that an inference from established facts is, by its nature, always a question of law. The court held that an inference from facts is a question of fact, unless the point for determination is a mixed question of law and fact. To hold otherwise, the court reasoned, would erase the distinction between questions of law and fact and improperly allow courts to review all factual determinations on appeal, which would defeat the legislative policy of limiting such reviews.

issue.issue_text: Whether a finding of fact can be challenged as an error of law if it is unsupported by any evidence or is unreasonable and perverse.

law.statement: A finding of fact can be challenged as an error of law under certain limited circumstances.
The specific circumstances for such a challenge are when the finding is (1) not supported by any evidence, or (2) is unreasonable and perverse in nature.
A finding is considered unreasonable or perverse if no reasonable person could have come to that conclusion based on the evidence presented.
However, if there is some evidence to consider, the finding of a tribunal remains final. A court cannot overturn it simply because it would have been inclined to take a different view of the facts.
Misappreciation of evidence is not equivalent to a lack of evidence and does not constitute an error of law.

application.law_applied: A finding of fact can be challenged as an error of law under certain limited circumstances.
application.application_text: The Court reviewed numerous English and Privy Council decisions to establish the principle that while findings of pure fact are generally not to be disturbed, there is an exception.

application.law_applied: The specific circumstances for such a challenge are when the finding is (1) not supported by any evidence, or (2) is unreasonable and perverse in nature.
application.application_text: The Court cited and adopted the standard summarized in one case: "the court should take that course if it appears that the Commissioners have acted without any evidence or upon a view of the facts which could not reasonably be entertained".

application.law_applied: However, if there is some evidence to consider, the finding of a tribunal remains final. A court cannot overturn it simply because it would have been inclined to take a different view of the facts.
application.application_text: The Court explicitly distinguished this narrow exception from a general right of appeal on facts. It stated that "where there is evidence to consider the finding of the Tribunal does not cease to be final simply because the Court may be inclined to take a view different from that of the Tribunal." This limitation is crucial to maintain the distinction between questions of fact and questions of law.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, establishing that a finding of fact can be challenged as an error of law, but only in the exceptional circumstances where the finding is completely unsupported by any evidence or is so unreasonable and perverse that no rational person could have reached it. The Court clarified that this does not permit a reviewing court to simply substitute its own judgment on the evidence for that of the original tribunal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an inference from established facts is, by its nature, a question of law and therefore open to review by the court.
appellant_arguments: Whenever a tribunal finds certain basic facts and then states its conclusions based on them, the determination of that conclusion is a question of law.
The court has the authority to review the conclusions drawn by the tribunal from the evidence and determine if they are justified.
respondent_arguments: An inference drawn from basic findings of fact is itself a conclusion of fact and is binding on the court.
If a tribunal states its conclusions on the facts, intending them to be their determination, those determinations are findings of fact and not open to review.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a finding of fact can be challenged as an error of law if it is unsupported by any evidence or is unreasonable and perverse.
appellant_arguments: The finding of the Tribunal that the intermediary firms were benamidars for the appellant was not supported by any legal evidence.

The facts relied upon by the Tribunal were neutral and did not justify the conclusion; the evidence was misinterpreted and given undue weight (e.g., the significance of partners being from a trading community).
respondent_arguments: The appellant's challenge is not about a lack of evidence but is merely a disagreement with the appreciation and weight of the evidence, which is not a question of law.
The finding is justified by the combination of circumstances, even if individual facts, in isolation, might seem neutral.

cases.principle: When a tribunal states the evidence before it and then adds its conclusion based on that evidence, it is open to the court to determine whether the evidence justified the conclusion drawn by the tribunal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An inference from facts is a question of law only when it is a mixed question of law and fact, where the ultimate finding is derived from applying legal principles to the established facts. In contrast, a finding on a pure question of fact, even if it is an inference from other basic facts, is not a question of law and is not subject to review, unless it is unsupported by any evidence or is so unreasonable that no rational person could have reached that conclusion.
obiter: To take an illustration, let us suppose that in a suit on a promissory note the defence taken is one of denial of execution. The court finds that the disputed signature is unlike the admitted signatures of the defendant. It also finds that the attesting witnesses who speak to execution were not, in fact, present at the time of the alleged execution. On a consideration of these facts, the court comes to the conclusion that the promissory note is not genuine.

why_appellant_lost: Can it be said that a conclusion of fact, pure and simple, ceases to be that when it is in tutu a deduc- tion from other facts? What can be the principle on which a question oi fact becomes transformed into a question oflaw when it involves an inference from basic facts?

if the appellant's contention is correct, then a finding of fact must, when it is an inference from other facts, be open to consideration not only on the ground that it is not supported by evidence or perverse but also on the ground that it is not a proper conclusion to come to on the facts. In other words, the jurisdiction in such cases is in the nature of a regular appeal on the correctness of the finding.
Nor do the observations made by the Privy Council in a number of cases lend any snpport tp the broad contention that inferences from facts are always and necessarily question• of law.
why_respondent_won: Considering the question on principle, when there is a question of fact to be determined it would usually be necessary first to decide disputed facts of a subsi- diary or evidentiary character, and the ultimate con- clusion will depend on an appreciation of these facts. Can it be said that a conclusion of fact, pure and simple, ceases to be that when it is in tutu a deduc- tion from other facts?

This decision, therefore, is no authority for the position that where a finding is given on a question of fact based upon an inference from facts, that is always a question of law, and the following observation of Lord Radcliffe at page 592 is directly against it

That will, in effect, be to wipe out the distinction between ques- tions of law and questions of fact and to defeat the policy underlying sections 66(1) and 66(2).
Dne should hesitate to accept a contention which leads to consequences so startling, unless there are com- pelling reasons therefor.
